before.title: Where it started and where it is now
before.text: A neuroendocrine tumour (NET) starts in cells that receive signals and can release hormones. The original organ is the primary site. A pancreatic NET is different from the more common pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Stage describes how far the cancer has spread; the stage system depends on its original site. A tumour in the liver may be a NET that spread there from elsewhere.

after.title: Where it started and where it is now
after.text: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.

before.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
before.text: Differentiation describes how the cells look under the microscope. Grade describes their growth activity. Ki-67 is a laboratory measure of the proportion of tumour cells showing a marker of cell growth and helps assess grade in relevant NETs. It is not the percentage of your body affected and is not a survival percentage. Ask for the exact pathology wording, grade and Ki-67 result, including the sample date.

after.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
after.text: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.

before.title: Grade is different from stage
before.text: A low-grade NET can have spread, and a high-grade tumour is not automatically stage 4. Well-differentiated grade 3 NET and poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are different diagnoses with different treatment choices. These medicine guides must not be applied to another diagnosis simply because its name contains neuroendocrine.

after.title: Grade is different from stage
after.text: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.

before.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
before.text: A functioning NET causes a hormone-related syndrome. A nonfunctioning NET does not cause a recognisable excess-hormone syndrome, but it can still grow or cause symptoms by its size or location. Ask which description applies to you. A positive somatostatin receptor scan does not by itself mean the tumour is functioning.

after.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
after.text: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.

before.title: Your diagnosis record
before.text: Keep the primary site, differentiation, grade, Ki-67 if reported, stage or sites of spread, hormone syndrome and receptor-scan result together in your passport. Ask the team to explain changes rather than trying to interpret one result in isolation.

after.title: Your diagnosis record
after.text: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.

before.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
before.text: Blood counts measure infection-fighting cells, oxygen-carrying cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests help the team assess how your body can handle treatment. The schedule for your medicine is shown separately. Attend these checks even when you feel well; a scan does not replace them.

after.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
after.text: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.

before.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
before.text: CT and MRI help show tumour size and where it is. A somatostatin receptor (SSTR) scan looks for receptor targets that certain treatments can attach to. An FDG-PET scan answers a different question about tumour activity and may be useful in selected cases. You will not necessarily need every scan. The specialist decides which test can change your care.

after.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
after.text: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.

before.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
before.text: The team may measure selected blood or urine markers when they answer a question about your NET or symptoms. These can include serotonin-related testing such as 5-HIAA for selected patients, or specific pancreatic hormones. Chromogranin A is not a universal test before every treatment. A changing marker alone does not prove cancer growth. Record why each test is being done, how to prepare and who will explain it.

after.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
after.text: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.

before.title: Preparing for a test
before.text: Ask whether you need fasting, a timed urine collection, dietary preparation or a medicine review. Follow the laboratory’s instructions for your particular test. Do not stop an acid-suppressing medicine, diabetes medicine or hormone-control treatment yourself. Tell the team about kidney problems, allergies and all medicines before a scan or blood test.

after.title: Preparing for a test
after.text: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.

before.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
before.text: A heart ultrasound may be needed for particular treatment risks or to assess heart-valve problems associated with a hormone syndrome. It is not required on the same timetable for every NET. Depending on the diagnosis, age and family history, the team may offer genetic counselling; some NETs occur with inherited conditions such as MEN1. A tumour gene test and an inherited-risk test are not interchangeable.

after.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
after.text: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.

before.title: Who does what, and when?
before.text: Use the passport to write each test, its purpose, planned date, booking service, result-review contact and next step. Your consultant sets response-scan and marker intervals. The postoperative schedules in general guides are not automatically the right schedule while you are taking these medicines.

after.title: Who does what, and when?
after.text: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.

before.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
before.text: Record your usual bowel pattern, flushing, pain, appetite, weight and energy before starting. Note what changes, how long it lasts, what you were taking and how it affects daily life. This helps the team distinguish a hormone problem from treatment toxicity without assuming that every symptom is cancer progression.

after.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
after.text: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.

before.title: Hormone-related symptoms
before.text: Depending on the tumour, excess hormones may cause flushing, frequent watery stools, wheezing, acid-related pain or blood-sugar disturbances. An insulin-producing tumour can cause low blood sugar. Not every NET causes these problems. Ask which symptoms matter for your diagnosis and whether you need a separate rescue plan.

after.title: Hormone-related symptoms
after.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

before.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
before.text: Somatostatin analogue injections and other symptom treatments may continue alongside anticancer treatment when prescribed. They may have their own appointment dates. Never stop them simply because tablets are paused. PRRT requires a carefully coordinated interruption and restart plan, which the nuclear-medicine service must supply.

after.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
after.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

before.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
before.text: Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic or imaging team if you have a hormone-producing NET or a previous hormone crisis. Ask your specialist whether special preparation is needed. Carry your current medicines and emergency plan; the wallet card supports this information but does not replace specialist instructions.

after.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
after.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

before.title: What are we trying to achieve?
before.text: Ask whether the main aim is to slow growth, reduce tumour size, relieve hormone symptoms, make another treatment possible or protect day-to-day quality of life. The aim and likely benefit depend on your particular NET and previous treatment. A stable scan may represent useful control even without tumour shrinkage.

after.title: What are we trying to achieve?
after.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

before.title: How treatments fit together
before.text: Some people need surgery, hormone-control treatment, tablets, chemotherapy, PRRT, liver-directed treatment or external radiotherapy at different points. These are not all automatically part of your regimen. Ask the multidisciplinary team to draw your own sequence and name the clinician coordinating it.

after.title: How treatments fit together
after.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

before.title: Choosing between options
before.text: Ask why this option suits your tumour site, grade, growth rate, symptoms, receptor status and other health conditions. Discuss alternatives, the option of observation when appropriate, supportive care, and any suitable clinical trial. A treatment listed in a US guide is not a guarantee of availability or funding in Ireland.

after.title: Choosing between options
after.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

before.title: Evidence is about groups
before.text: A trial can measure time before cancer worsens, tumour shrinkage or survival. These are different outcomes. A group result does not predict your own response or lifespan. Ask how closely the study patients match your diagnosis and what benefit would make the treatment worthwhile to you.

after.title: Evidence is about groups
after.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

before.title: Review points and shared decisions
before.text: Agree when you will review symptoms, tests and scans, and what would lead to continuing, delaying, changing or stopping treatment. Discuss work, caring duties, travel and the effects you most want to avoid. You can revisit your choices as your situation changes.

after.title: Review points and shared decisions
after.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

before.title: Food, weight and digestion
before.text: Tell the team about weight loss, poor appetite, early fullness, persistent diarrhoea or greasy stools. Ask for a dietitian familiar with NETs and your surgery or medicines. Different causes need different support; do not assume every bowel symptom needs the same diet or medicine. Ask whether digestive-enzyme assessment or replacement is relevant to you.

after.title: Food, weight and digestion
after.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

before.title: Fluids and safe activity
before.text: Follow your individual fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea, kidney disease or heart problems. Balance manageable activity with rest. Tell the team if fatigue, dizziness, pain or breathlessness limits usual tasks; these symptoms can have treatable causes.

after.title: Fluids and safe activity
after.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

before.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
before.text: Living with repeated tests and treatment can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Ask about psychological support, sexual health, fertility advice, symptom-control services and support for carers. Supportive or palliative care aims to improve comfort and daily life and can accompany active anticancer treatment.

after.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
after.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

before.title: Practical help
before.text: Ask your nurse or social worker about transport, work, finances, home support, caring responsibilities and local NET support organisations. A general resource list may include services in other countries; your team can identify options available to you.

after.title: Practical help
after.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

before.title: A record that works without a phone
before.text: Keep the printed schedule, medicine list, tests, contact numbers and written emergency instructions together. The full handbook contains the information in sequence for offline reading. The QR code is an optional route to more information; it is not needed to call for help or follow your paper plan.

after.title: A record that works without a phone
after.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

before.title: Questions to take to the next visit
before.text: What is my exact diagnosis and grade? What is treatment trying to achieve? Which tests are mandatory for this medicine, and which depend on my NET? Who reviews results? What symptoms mean call now? What support would help me live as well as possible?

after.title: Questions to take to the next visit
after.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

before.name: Dabrafenib
before.explanation: A BRAF V600 change can keep the cell-growth pathway switched on. Dabrafenib blocks the altered BRAF protein. It is paired with a MEK inhibitor to act on the same pathway at another point. The BRAF result comes from tumour testing; it does not automatically mean a hereditary condition.
before.watch: Fever needs the written hold/contact plan. Check other medicines and contraception because interactions can matter.
risks: Fever and chills, dehydration
Skin rash and new skin tumours
Headache, fatigue and joint pain
Eye inflammation
Bleeding and liver changes
Harm to pregnancy and drug interactions

after.name: Dabrafenib
after.explanation: Dabrafenib inhibits an altered BRAF protein that sends growth signals inside eligible melanoma cells. Trametinib blocks another step in that pathway. The tumour’s BRAF result is checked before selecting this treatment.
after.watch: Fever needs the written hold/contact plan. Check other medicines and contraception because interactions can matter.
risks: Fever and chills, dehydration
Skin rash and new skin tumours
Headache, fatigue and joint pain
Eye inflammation
Bleeding and liver changes
Harm to pregnancy and drug interactions

before.name: Trametinib
before.explanation: MEK carries growth signals further along the pathway below BRAF. Trametinib blocks MEK alongside dabrafenib. Normal heart, eye, lung and other tissues can also be affected, which is why scheduled tests and prompt symptom reporting matter.
before.watch: Attend cardiac tests. New eye symptoms, cough, breathlessness, swelling or severe diarrhoea need prompt review.
risks: Reduced heart pumping function
Retinal and other eye problems
Lung inflammation
Diarrhoea, swelling and rash
Bleeding, liver changes and muscle injury
Harm to pregnancy

after.name: Trametinib
after.explanation: Trametinib inhibits MEK proteins, which pass growth signals onward inside cells. It is used with dabrafenib in this plan. Normal tissues can also be affected, so heart checks and prompt reporting of eye or breathing symptoms remain important.
after.watch: Attend cardiac tests. New eye symptoms, cough, breathlessness, swelling or severe diarrhoea need prompt review.
risks: Reduced heart pumping function
Retinal and other eye problems
Lung inflammation
Diarrhoea, swelling and rash
Bleeding, liver changes and muscle injury
Harm to pregnancy

before.title: Eating, activity and practical help
before.text: Report falling intake, weight loss, pain or fatigue early. The team can tailor nutrition, activity, wound, psychological and practical support to your needs.

after.title: Eating, activity and practical help
after.text: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

before.title: Required safety checks and your individual disease-assessment plan

Regular skin reviews are required; your oncology team will confirm and record the interval. Head/neck examination every three months and chest CT every six months are specified surveillance checks; disease-response imaging follows the individual plan.
Contact the team for new symptoms; extra tests may be needed between scheduled checks.

Follow-up depends on stage, treatment and symptoms. Your team records the skin/lymph-node examination plan, whether body or brain imaging is needed, and which service owns each appointment. A general patient booklet does not set a universal scan interval for every patient.

Review treatment taken or received, holds, adverse effects and supportive medicines.

Use an effective alternative to hormonal contraception during treatment and for two weeks after dabrafenib and 16 weeks after trametinib; dabrafenib can make hormonal contraception less effective. The team must confirm the method and the later applicable end date for the combination. Do not breastfeed during treatment; ask when it is safe to resume. Report a possible pregnancy promptly.

before.title: Appointments and supply
before.text: Arrange dates, medicine supply, transport and any needed interpreter or carer support. Ask whether bloods are taken in the oncology unit or elsewhere and how the result reaches the prescriber.

after.title: Appointments and supply
after.text: Plan blood tests, travel and medicine collection in advance. If you need an interpreter or someone to help at home, tell the team before the appointment.

before.title: Paper copies and contact information
before.text: Keep this complete handbook, the three-page summary and the wallet card together. The QR code is optional. Ask the team to add your actual contacts and print a revised plan when treatment changes.

after.title: Paper copies and contact information
after.text: Ask for your latest schedule and contact details on paper. Replace old versions when treatment changes so everyone helping you uses the same plan.

before.title: What the evidence means for your treatment
before.intro: The evidence discussion must match the diagnosis, biomarker and treatment setting shown in this guide.
before.population: NCCP 00415b: adjuvant treatment after complete resection of stage III melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation. This route is distinct from treatment of unresectable or metastatic melanoma.
before.interpretation: Ask which outcomes matter in your setting and what benefit is realistic for you. No survival percentage from another regimen, dose combination or disease setting is assigned here.
limitations: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
The supplied NCCN patient guide is an education reference, not Irish prescribing or reimbursement authority.
This handoff does not claim a completed independent quantitative trial-benefit audit.

after.title: What the evidence means for your treatment
after.intro: Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.
after.population: NCCP 00415b: adjuvant treatment after complete resection of stage III melanoma with a BRAF V600 mutation. This route is distinct from treatment of unresectable or metastatic melanoma.
after.interpretation: Ask which outcomes matter in your setting and what benefit is realistic for you. No survival percentage from another regimen, dose combination or disease setting is assigned here.
limitations: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
Your team explains the evidence that applies to this treatment plan and the uncertainty for you as an individual.

before.title: What the diagnosis says
before.text: Keep the pathology summary, original skin site, stage and details of any lymph-node involvement together. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the original melanoma; they are different from the stage. If the diagnosis arose in the eye or a mucosal surface, ask whether this cutaneous-melanoma information applies.

after.title: What the diagnosis says
after.text: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

before.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
before.text: A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether the BRAF/MEK targeted medicines in this guide are suitable. This is usually a test of the tumour, not proof of an inherited family condition. Keep the actual result and test date; ask about genetic counselling only when your personal or family history makes that relevant.

after.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
after.text: A BRAF V600 result identifies whether the targeted medicines in this plan can act on the tumour. Keep the laboratory result and date. A tumour change is not, on its own, evidence of an inherited condition.

before.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
before.text: Record what surgery removed and whether the present medicine is postoperative treatment to lower recurrence risk or treatment of cancer that remains or has spread. Radiotherapy, stereotactic treatment or another operation may have a separate role; their timing and side effects need their own plan.

after.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
after.text: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

before.title: Stage and response are different
before.text: Stage describes the extent of melanoma at diagnosis or a later reassessment. A response assessment asks how known cancer has changed with treatment. In the adjuvant setting there may be no visible tumour to measure: surveillance looks for recurrence while safety checks look for medicine effects.

after.title: Stage and response are different
after.text: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

before.title: A new skin change still needs review
before.text: Continue to report a new or changing mole, a non-healing lesion, a new lump or an unexplained persistent symptom. Do not assume every new lesion is melanoma, and do not use a photograph or a good response at one site to rule out a problem elsewhere.

after.title: A new skin change still needs review
after.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

before.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
before.text: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.

after.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
after.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

before.title: Practical preparation
before.text: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.

after.title: Practical preparation
after.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

before.title: Getting the result
before.text: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.

after.title: Getting the result
after.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

before.title: Eating, drinking and activity
before.text: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.

after.title: Eating, drinking and activity
after.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

before.title: Protect your skin
before.text: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.

after.title: Protect your skin
after.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

before.title: Know the pattern of your skin
before.text: Ask how to examine your skin, scars and relevant lymph-node areas and how often your own team recommends doing so. A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.

after.title: Know the pattern of your skin
after.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

before.title: Photographs are optional
before.text: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.

after.title: Photographs are optional
after.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

before.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
before.text: Use the dressings and skin-care plan recommended for your lesion and treatment. Ask before applying new creams or remedies to an open or treated area. Worsening pain, discharge, redness, bleeding or loss of function needs advice; routine skin-care instructions are not a substitute for assessment.

after.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
after.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

before.title: Benefits and uncertainties
before.text: Ask what evidence applies to your diagnosis, stage, biomarker and treatment setting, what outcome the team hopes to improve, and what may happen without this treatment. A trial average cannot predict an individual result; a benefit measured in one setting should not be transferred to another.

after.title: Benefits and uncertainties
after.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

before.title: Alternatives and review points
before.text: Discuss other suitable treatments, clinical trials if relevant, local treatment options and symptom-focused care. Ask when the decision will be reviewed and what would prompt a change. Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life alongside anticancer treatment.

after.title: Alternatives and review points
after.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

before.title: Help with daily life
before.text: Tell the team about work, transport, caring responsibilities, cost concerns, body image, anxiety or sleep. Ask which nurse, social worker, dietitian, rehabilitation professional or support organisation can help. Use resources relevant to your country and service; a US guide may describe different access or funding.

before.intro: The evidence discussion must match the diagnosis, biomarker and treatment setting shown in this guide.
before.population: Completely resected stage IIB/IIC or stage III cutaneous melanoma; the team confirms the applicable NCCP indication and timing.

before.title: What the diagnosis says
before.text: Keep the pathology summary, original skin site, stage and details of any lymph-node involvement together. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the original melanoma; they are different from the stage. If the diagnosis arose in the eye or a mucosal surface, ask whether this cutaneous-melanoma information applies.

after.title: What the diagnosis says
after.text: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

before.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
before.text: A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether the BRAF/MEK targeted medicines as a separate treatment option from the immunotherapy described in this guide are suitable. This is usually a test of the tumour, not proof of an inherited family condition. Keep the actual result and test date; ask about genetic counselling only when your personal or family history makes that relevant.

after.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
after.text: BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.

before.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
before.text: Record what surgery removed and whether the present medicine is postoperative treatment to lower recurrence risk or treatment of cancer that remains or has spread. Radiotherapy, stereotactic treatment or another operation may have a separate role; their timing and side effects need their own plan.

after.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
after.text: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

before.title: Stage and response are different
before.text: Stage describes the extent of melanoma at diagnosis or a later reassessment. A response assessment asks how known cancer has changed with treatment. In the adjuvant setting there may be no visible tumour to measure: surveillance looks for recurrence while safety checks look for medicine effects.

after.title: Stage and response are different
after.text: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

before.title: A new skin change still needs review
before.text: Continue to report a new or changing mole, a non-healing lesion, a new lump or an unexplained persistent symptom. Do not assume every new lesion is melanoma, and do not use a photograph or a good response at one site to rule out a problem elsewhere.

after.title: A new skin change still needs review
after.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

before.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
before.text: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.

after.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
after.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

before.title: Practical preparation
before.text: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.

after.title: Practical preparation
after.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

before.title: Getting the result
before.text: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.

after.title: Getting the result
after.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

before.title: Eating, drinking and activity
before.text: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.

after.title: Eating, drinking and activity
after.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

before.title: Protect your skin
before.text: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.

after.title: Protect your skin
after.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

before.title: Know the pattern of your skin
before.text: Ask how to examine your skin, scars and relevant lymph-node areas and how often your own team recommends doing so. A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.

after.title: Know the pattern of your skin
after.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

before.title: Photographs are optional
before.text: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.

after.title: Photographs are optional
after.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

before.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin

after.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
after.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

before.title: Benefits and uncertainties

A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.

after.title: Know the pattern of your skin
after.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

before.title: Photographs are optional
before.text: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.

after.title: Photographs are optional
after.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

before.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
before.text: Use the dressings and skin-care plan recommended for your lesion and treatment. Ask before applying new creams or remedies to an open or treated area. Worsening pain, discharge, redness, bleeding or loss of function needs advice; routine skin-care instructions are not a substitute for assessment.

after.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
after.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

before.title: Benefits and uncertainties
before.text: Ask what evidence applies to your diagnosis, stage, biomarker and treatment setting, what outcome the team hopes to improve, and what may happen without this treatment. A trial average cannot predict an individual result; a benefit measured in one setting should not be transferred to another.

after.title: Benefits and uncertainties
after.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

before.title: Alternatives and review points
before.text: Discuss other suitable treatments, clinical trials if relevant, local treatment options and symptom-focused care. Ask when the decision will be reviewed and what would prompt a change. Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life alongside anticancer treatment.

after.title: Alternatives and review points
after.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

before.title: Help with daily life
before.text: Tell the team about work, transport, caring responsibilities, cost concerns, body image, anxiety or sleep. Ask which nurse, social worker, dietitian, rehabilitation professional or support organisation can help. Use resources relevant to your country and service; a US guide may describe different access or funding.

after.title: Help with daily life
after.text: Tell the team what is hardest in daily life: travel, work, caring duties, costs, sleep or confidence. Ask who can help and how to contact them.

before.title: Shared understanding
before.text: Ask someone on the team to check that you can explain the medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route in your own words. An interpreter, large-print copy or a trusted supporter can help; none requires you to use a smartphone.

after.title: Shared understanding
after.text: Before going home, check that you can describe your medicine schedule, next tests and urgent-contact route. Ask for an interpreter, larger print or a supporter if that would help.

before.title: Your follow-up plan
before.text: Follow-up depends on stage, treatment and symptoms. Your team records the skin/lymph-node examination plan, whether body or brain imaging is needed, and which service owns each appointment. A general patient booklet does not set a universal scan interval for every patient.

after.title: Your follow-up plan
after.text: Your stage, symptoms and treatment determine follow-up. Write down the skin and lymph-node checks, any body or brain scans and the service arranging them. Confirm your own dates with the team.

before.title: The complete paper version
before.text: This handbook can be used without a phone: keep the schedule, symptom advice, medicine list, tests and contacts together. The QR code is an optional route to the matching regimen information. Ask the team to print updates when your plan changes and keep the latest dated copy.

after.title: The complete paper version
after.text: Use this handbook as your paper record. Keep the current schedule, medicines, tests and contacts together, and replace outdated pages after a change. The matching QR link is optional.

before.name: Pembrolizumab
before.explanation: Pembrolizumab blocks PD-1, a signal that can reduce T-cell activity. This can help immune cells act against melanoma, but it can also allow inflammation in healthy organs. It is not conventional chemotherapy, and side effects can occur after treatment stops.
before.watch: Carry your immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms early, including after treatment ends.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver or kidneys
Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal and glucose problems
Skin reactions and rare severe skin injury
Rare heart, muscle, neurological and eye inflammation
Infusion reactions
Some immune effects need long-term treatment

after.name: Pembrolizumab
after.explanation: Pembrolizumab blocks the PD-1 checkpoint, allowing T cells to remain more active against cancer. Immune activity can also affect normal organs, so new symptoms matter during treatment and after it stops.
after.watch: Carry your immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms early, including after treatment ends.
risks: Immune inflammation of bowel, lungs, liver or kidneys
Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal and glucose problems
Skin reactions and rare severe skin injury
Rare heart, muscle, neurological and eye inflammation
Infusion reactions
Some immune effects need long-term treatment

before.title: Eating, activity and practical help
before.text: Report falling intake, weight loss, pain or fatigue early. The team can tailor nutrition, activity, wound, psychological and practical support to your needs.

after.title: Eating, activity and practical help
after.text: Let the team know if cramps, altered taste or poor appetite make eating or moving difficult. Ask for practical food and activity advice that fits your symptoms and any other illness.

before.title: Required safety checks and your individual disease-assessment plan

rows.label: Bloods and organ safety
cells: Blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and thyroid tests; review autoimmune conditions, transplants, previous immune reactions and all current medicines.

Blood count, kidney/liver tests and glucose before every 3-week cycle. TSH is checked every 3–6 weeks, including between treatment visits when needed. Cortisol and other tests are added when clinically indicated. Report new symptoms at every visit and between visits; normal blood results do not rule out immune toxicity.
Contact the team for new symptoms; extra tests may be needed between scheduled checks.
Safety bloods do not by themselves show whether cancer is responding.

Continue to report possible immune effects after the last dose; your team records the follow-up tests and dates. Keep any prescribed steroid taper, hormone replacement and specialist follow-up. Scans follow your individual disease plan.

rows.label: Cancer, skin and daily function
cells: Record diagnosis, stage, current disease sites and the baseline assessment.
Keep the source-specific skin and clinical reviews and the individually agreed response assessments.
Record new lesions, lumps, wound changes, pain and effects on usual activities.
Write the next examination or scan date and the responsible team; no universal scan or tumour-marker interval is assumed.

Follow-up depends on stage, treatment and symptoms. Your team records the skin/lymph-node examination plan, whether body or brain imaging is needed, and which service owns each appointment. A general patient booklet does not set a universal scan interval for every patient.

rows.label: Medicines and continuing precautions
cells: Review all medicines and the pregnancy/fertility plan.
Review treatment taken or received, holds, adverse effects and supportive medicines.
Keep the actual urgent contacts and do not restart a held medicine yourself.
Bring the medicine list and treatment summary to other services.

Discuss fertility before starting. Use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 4 months after the last dose. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy. Discuss breastfeeding restrictions with the team before treatment; do not breastfeed without their advice. Do not stop prescribed steroids or hormone replacement yourself.

before.title: Paper copies and contact information

after.title: Paper copies and contact information

before.title: What the evidence means for your treatment
before.intro: The evidence discussion must match the diagnosis, biomarker and treatment setting shown in this guide.
before.population: Selected stage IIIB melanoma eligible for the NCCP adjuvant indication: the treating clinician may choose pembrolizumab 200 mg before and after surgery. This is a distinct, discretionary perioperative plan.
before.interpretation: Evidence in advanced melanoma measures control of existing cancer; adjuvant evidence measures recurrence after surgery. Perioperative evidence concerns treatment around surgery. Ask which study and outcome match your stage and plan. These results cannot predict your individual benefit.
limitations: Individual benefit and risk cannot be predicted from a group average.
The NCCN patient reference supports education; the current NCCP indication governs this Irish regimen.

after.intro: Discuss the evidence for your diagnosis, tumour test results and treatment setting.

before.title: What the diagnosis says
before.text: Keep the pathology summary, original skin site, stage and details of any lymph-node involvement together. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the original melanoma; they are different from the stage. If the diagnosis arose in the eye or a mucosal surface, ask whether this cutaneous-melanoma information applies.

after.title: What the diagnosis says
after.text: Record the original melanoma site and pathology findings. Breslow thickness and ulceration describe features of the skin tumour; stage describes its extent. Melanoma arising in the eye or a mucosal surface may need a different pathway.

before.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
before.text: A BRAF V600 result helps decide whether the BRAF/MEK targeted medicines as a separate treatment option from the immunotherapy described in this guide are suitable. This is usually a test of the tumour, not proof of an inherited family condition. Keep the actual result and test date; ask about genetic counselling only when your personal or family history makes that relevant.

after.title: BRAF and other tumour tests
after.text: BRAF V600 testing can identify an alternative targeted-treatment option in some melanomas. It is separate from the immunotherapy described here. Ask what your tumour result means for the choices available to you.

before.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
before.text: Record what surgery removed and whether the present medicine is postoperative treatment to lower recurrence risk or treatment of cancer that remains or has spread. Radiotherapy, stereotactic treatment or another operation may have a separate role; their timing and side effects need their own plan.

after.title: Surgery, radiotherapy and medicine have different roles
after.text: Ask whether medicine is intended to reduce recurrence after complete surgery or control cancer that remains. Add any operation or radiotherapy to the plan with its own purpose, timing and risks.

before.title: Stage and response are different
before.text: Stage describes the extent of melanoma at diagnosis or a later reassessment. A response assessment asks how known cancer has changed with treatment. In the adjuvant setting there may be no visible tumour to measure: surveillance looks for recurrence while safety checks look for medicine effects.

after.title: Stage and response are different
after.text: Stage describes the extent of disease. Response describes a change in measurable cancer during treatment. After complete removal there may be no visible tumour to measure; follow-up then looks for recurrence and treatment effects.

before.title: A new skin change still needs review
before.text: Continue to report a new or changing mole, a non-healing lesion, a new lump or an unexplained persistent symptom. Do not assume every new lesion is melanoma, and do not use a photograph or a good response at one site to rule out a problem elsewhere.

after.title: A new skin change still needs review
after.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

before.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
before.text: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.

after.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
after.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

before.title: Practical preparation
before.text: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.

after.title: Practical preparation
after.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

before.title: Getting the result
before.text: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.

after.title: Getting the result
after.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

before.title: Eating, drinking and activity
before.text: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.

after.title: Eating, drinking and activity
after.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

before.text: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.

before.title: A new skin change still needs review

after.title: A new skin change still needs review
after.text: Report a new or changing mole, a sore that persists, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. A photo or a good response in one area cannot rule out a separate problem.

before.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
before.text: Record surgery, radiotherapy and other anticancer medicines separately, including dates and the specialist responsible. This schedule does not automatically include or authorise another treatment. Ask whether any overlap changes tests, symptoms to report or the timing of appointments.

after.title: The role of earlier or later treatment
after.text: Ask how the medicine fits with previous or planned local treatment. The timing of an operation, radiotherapy and a tablet course should be written in one agreed plan.

before.title: Practical preparation
before.text: Arrange medicine supply, transport, interpreter or carer support before it is needed. Bring the alert card, symptom record and questions. Ask which appointments require someone to accompany you and how to obtain urgent advice outside normal hours.

after.title: Practical preparation
after.text: Bring your medicine list, allergy information and questions. Tell the team about practical problems with travel, swallowing, wound care or remembering doses before treatment starts.

before.title: Getting the result
before.text: For each test, record its purpose, due date, result and action. Agree how results reach you and who checks a result from another hospital. If an appointment or result has not arrived, contact the named service rather than assuming no news means no action is needed.

after.title: Getting the result
after.text: Keep a named contact for bookings and results. If an expected appointment or result is missing, call that service; do not take silence as confirmation that everything is complete.

before.title: Eating, drinking and activity
before.text: Tell the team early about nausea, taste change, a sore mouth, diarrhoea or falling weight. Ask for an individual fluid and food plan if heart, kidney or other conditions limit intake. Gentle activity and planned rest can help maintain function; adjust to symptoms and ask for support when fatigue limits daily life.

after.title: Eating, drinking and activity
after.text: Report nausea, mouth discomfort, diarrhoea or weight loss before they make eating and drinking difficult. The team can adjust symptom support and arrange dietitian or rehabilitation advice.

before.title: Protect your skin
before.text: Use shade, protective clothing, a hat and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, and avoid tanning beds. Reapply sunscreen according to its instructions. Protection matters even when it is cloudy; choose a practical approach that lets you remain active safely.

after.title: Protect your skin
after.text: Protect exposed skin with clothing, a hat and shade. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and reapply as directed. Avoid sunbeds. Cloudy weather does not remove ultraviolet exposure.

before.title: Know the pattern of your skin
before.text: Ask how to examine your skin, scars and relevant lymph-node areas and how often your own team recommends doing so. A mirror or a trusted helper can make hard-to-see areas easier to check. Report a new or changing lesion, a non-healing sore or a new lump rather than waiting for a routine visit.

after.title: Know the pattern of your skin
after.text: Ask the team to show you how to check your skin and treated area. Use a mirror or a helper for areas you cannot see. Report a new lump, a changing lesion or a sore that does not heal.

before.title: Photographs are optional
before.text: If useful, keep a dated photograph with consistent lighting and a size reference, following your team’s advice. Photographs are optional and do not diagnose a cancer or replace examination. Keep them privately; this printable passport does not require you to upload images or other personal health information.

after.title: Photographs are optional
after.text: A private, dated photograph can help describe a change if your team finds it useful. Keep the lighting and size reference consistent. Photographs support a discussion; they do not replace examination and need not be uploaded.

before.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
before.text: Use the dressings and skin-care plan recommended for your lesion and treatment. Ask before applying new creams or remedies to an open or treated area. after.title: Wounds, nails and sensitive skin
after.text: Follow the wound and skin-care instructions for the treated area. Ask before adding a cream or remedy. Increasing redness, discharge, pain, bleeding or difficulty using the area needs assessment.

before.title: Benefits and uncertainties
before.text: Ask what evidence applies to your diagnosis, stage, biomarker and treatment setting, what outcome the team hopes to improve, and what may happen without this treatment. after.title: Benefits and uncertainties
after.text: Ask what outcome this treatment aims to improve for your diagnosis and what alternatives exist. Results from a study group help a discussion but cannot promise your own result.

before.title: Alternatives and review points

after.title: Alternatives and review points
after.text: Agree the next decision point and what would make the plan change. Ask about other suitable treatments, trials and symptom care. Support for comfort and function can continue alongside cancer treatment.

before.title: Help with daily life
before.text: Tell the team about work, transport, caring responsibilities, cost concerns, body image, anxiety or sleep. Use resources relevant to your country and service; a US guide may describe different access or funding.

after.title: Help with daily life

after.title: Shared understanding

before.title: Your follow-up plan
