after.title: Hormone-related symptoms
after.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

before.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
before.text: Somatostatin analogue injections and other symptom treatments may continue alongside anticancer treatment when prescribed. They may have their own appointment dates. Never stop them simply because tablets are paused. PRRT requires a carefully coordinated interruption and restart plan, which the nuclear-medicine service must supply.

after.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
after.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

before.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
before.text: Tell the surgical, dental, anaesthetic or imaging team if you have a hormone-producing NET or a previous hormone crisis. Ask your specialist whether special preparation is needed. Carry your current medicines and emergency plan; the wallet card supports this information but does not replace specialist instructions.

after.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
after.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

before.title: What are we trying to achieve?
before.text: Ask whether the main aim is to slow growth, reduce tumour size, relieve hormone symptoms, make another treatment possible or protect day-to-day quality of life. The aim and likely benefit depend on your particular NET and previous treatment. A stable scan may represent useful control even without tumour shrinkage.

after.title: What are we trying to achieve?
after.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

before.title: How treatments fit together
before.text: Some people need surgery, hormone-control treatment, tablets, chemotherapy, PRRT, liver-directed treatment or external radiotherapy at different points. These are not all automatically part of your regimen. Ask the multidisciplinary team to draw your own sequence and name the clinician coordinating it.

after.title: How treatments fit together
after.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

before.title: Choosing between options
before.text: Ask why this option suits your tumour site, grade, growth rate, symptoms, receptor status and other health conditions. Discuss alternatives, the option of observation when appropriate, supportive care, and any suitable clinical trial. A treatment listed in a US guide is not a guarantee of availability or funding in Ireland.

after.title: Choosing between options
after.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

before.title: Evidence is about groups
before.text: A trial can measure time before cancer worsens, tumour shrinkage or survival. These are different outcomes. A group result does not predict your own response or lifespan. Ask how closely the study patients match your diagnosis and what benefit would make the treatment worthwhile to you.

after.title: Evidence is about groups
after.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

before.title: Review points and shared decisions
before.text: Agree when you will review symptoms, tests and scans, and what would lead to continuing, delaying, changing or stopping treatment. Discuss work, caring duties, travel and the effects you most want to avoid. You can revisit your choices as your situation changes.

after.title: Review points and shared decisions
after.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

before.title: Food, weight and digestion
before.text: Tell the team about weight loss, poor appetite, early fullness, persistent diarrhoea or greasy stools. Ask for a dietitian familiar with NETs and your surgery or medicines. Different causes need different support; do not assume every bowel symptom needs the same diet or medicine. Ask whether digestive-enzyme assessment or replacement is relevant to you.

after.title: Food, weight and digestion
after.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

before.title: Fluids and safe activity
before.text: Follow your individual fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea, kidney disease or heart problems. Balance manageable activity with rest. Tell the team if fatigue, dizziness, pain or breathlessness limits usual tasks; these symptoms can have treatable causes.

after.title: Fluids and safe activity
after.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

before.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
before.text: Living with repeated tests and treatment can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Ask about psychological support, sexual health, fertility advice, symptom-control services and support for carers. Supportive or palliative care aims to improve comfort and daily life and can accompany active anticancer treatment.

after.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
after.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

before.title: Practical help
before.text: Ask your nurse or social worker about transport, work, finances, home support, caring responsibilities and local NET support organisations. A general resource list may include services in other countries; your team can identify options available to you.

after.title: Practical help
after.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

before.title: A record that works without a phone
before.text: Keep the printed schedule, medicine list, tests, contact numbers and written emergency instructions together. The full handbook contains the information in sequence for offline reading. The QR code is an optional route to more information; it is not needed to call for help or follow your paper plan.

after.title: A record that works without a phone
after.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

before.title: Questions to take to the next visit
before.text: What is my exact diagnosis and grade? What is treatment trying to achieve? Which tests are mandatory for this medicine, and which depend on my NET? Who reviews results? What symptoms mean call now? What support would help me live as well as possible?

after.title: Questions to take to the next visit
after.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

before.alias: External-beam treatment planned by radiation oncology
before.type: Treatment focused on the brain tumour area
before.mechanism: Damages DNA in the treated area
before.explanation: Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.
before.watch: Report new or worsening headache, vomiting, weakness, speech or memory change. The radiotherapy team gives a separate skin-care and symptom plan.

after.mechanism: Damages DNA in the treated area
after.explanation: Radiotherapy directs a planned dose of radiation to the tumour area. Radiation damages cellular DNA; planning aims to limit exposure of nearby healthy brain. The dose and treated area affect both benefit and side effects.
after.watch: Report new or worsening headache, vomiting, weakness, speech or memory change. The radiotherapy team gives a separate skin-care and symptom plan.

before.title: Steroid and seizure plans
before.text: Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

after.title: Steroid and seizure plans
after.text: If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

before.title: Help with the daily plan
before.text: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.

after.title: Help with the daily plan
after.text: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.

before.title: What each part does
before.text: Temozolomide crosses into the brain and creates chemical changes in DNA. If the damage cannot be repaired, a cell may stop dividing or die. Healthy blood-forming cells can also be affected, which helps explain blood-count changes, infection and bleeding risks. Nausea prevention and liver monitoring are important too. Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.

after.title: What each part does
after.text: Temozolomide produces chemical damage in DNA. Cells unable to repair that damage may stop dividing or die. Blood-forming cells can also be affected, which explains the need for blood counts and infection precautions. Radiotherapy damages DNA in the planned treatment area. Its team explains the separate dose, skin care and effects on the brain.

before.title: Help with the daily plan
before.text: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.

after.title: Help with the daily plan
after.text: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.

before.title: When to seek help
before.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

after.title: When to seek help
after.text: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

before.title: Support medicines
before.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. PJP-prevention medicine is required during temozolomide with radiotherapy in this NCCP regimen. Your team supplies the prescription and decides how long to continue, including if lymphocyte counts remain low. Do not stop it just because radiotherapy has finished. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

after.title: Support medicines
after.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. PJP-prevention medicine is required during temozolomide with radiotherapy in this NCCP regimen. Your team supplies the prescription and decides how long to continue, including if lymphocyte counts remain low. Do not stop it just because radiotherapy has finished. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

before.title: The name and location
before.text: Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different diagnoses. A tumour that spread to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and is not covered by these glioma regimens. Record the exact integrated diagnosis and where it is located.

after.title: The name and location
after.text: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.

before.title: Grade is not the same as stage
before.text: Grade describes features linked to how a tumour behaves. Adult gliomas are usually discussed by their type, grade and molecular findings rather than the stage system used for many other cancers. Grade 4 does not mean cancer has spread through the body. Ask your specialist to explain your own report and any older terminology in the treatment protocol.

after.title: Grade is not the same as stage
after.text: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.

before.title: IDH and 1p/19q
before.text: IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts of chromosomes 1p and 19q help classify particular gliomas. The combination of findings matters: one result should not be read in isolation. These tests are usually performed on tumour tissue. They do not automatically mean a change has been inherited or that relatives need testing.

after.title: IDH and 1p/19q
after.text: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.

before.title: MGMT promoter methylation
before.text: MGMT is involved in repairing certain DNA damage. Methylation of its promoter can reduce that repair activity and helps the team discuss the likely benefit of temozolomide in relevant settings. It is not a blood tumour marker, a percentage of tumour left, or an individual survival prediction. Record the reported result and ask how it affects your treatment choice.

after.title: MGMT promoter methylation
after.text: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.

before.title: A useful diagnosis record
before.text: Keep the biopsy or operation date, pathology wording, grade, IDH result, 1p/19q result and MGMT result if tested. Mark a result as pending or not applicable rather than assuming it is negative. Ask whether specialist pathology review or further testing would change the plan.

after.title: A useful diagnosis record
after.text: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.

before.title: Safety blood tests
before.text: A full blood count checks infection-fighting white cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets that help stop bleeding. Kidney and liver tests help assess treatment safety. Attend the regimen’s required tests even when you feel well; a reassuring scan does not replace them. The schedule in this guide separates checks before, during and after treatment.

after.title: Safety blood tests
after.text: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.

before.title: MRI and neurological review
before.text: MRI is the main scan used to assess many gliomas. Your team also considers symptoms, strength, movement, speech, memory, daily function and medicines such as steroids. Tell staff before MRI about implants or metal, kidney problems, previous contrast reactions or difficulty lying still. Ask about support if scans make you anxious.

after.title: MRI and neurological review
after.text: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.

before.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
before.text: After treatment, inflammation and other treatment effects can resemble tumour growth on MRI. This is sometimes called pseudoprogression. The team may need comparison scans, specialist imaging or further assessment before deciding what a change means. New or worsening symptoms still need prompt review; do not assume they are harmless treatment effects.

after.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
after.text: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.

before.title: An individual follow-up timetable
before.text: Write the next MRI date, what question it should answer and who will explain the result. Timing depends on your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous findings. General follow-up intervals in an international booklet are not automatically your schedule. These regimens do not require a generic CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or a blood tumour marker before every cycle.

after.title: An individual follow-up timetable
after.text: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.

before.title: Keep results with decisions
before.text: Use the passport to distinguish a test being booked, completed and reviewed. Record the agreed next step and whom to call if an appointment or result is missing. Do not alter chemotherapy or steroids yourself in response to a number or scan report.

after.title: Keep results with decisions
after.text: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.

before.title: Know your usual symptoms
before.text: Write down your usual headache, strength, walking, speech, vision, memory, mood, sleep and seizure pattern before treatment. Note new changes, when they started and how they affect daily tasks. With your permission, a trusted person can help spot changes or record what happened.

after.title: Know your usual symptoms
after.text: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

before.title: Urgent neurological changes
before.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.

after.title: Urgent neurological changes
after.text: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

before.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
before.text: Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swelling around the tumour. They are not automatically needed for everyone. Ask for the exact dose, time, review date and any taper plan. Do not stop or change them suddenly without advice. Report sleep or mood changes, increased thirst, infection symptoms or muscle weakness and ask which additional checks or protection you need.

after.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
after.text: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

before.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
before.text: If prescribed, take seizure medicines on the agreed schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and whom to contact for breakthrough symptoms. Some medicines can affect mood, alertness or interact with treatment. Do not start, stop or switch them yourself. A rescue medicine needs an individual plan and training for whoever may give it.

after.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
after.text: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

before.title: Safety at home and outside
before.text: Ask your clinical team about driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery in light of your symptoms and any seizures. Local medical and licensing rules need individual advice; this guide does not give a universal driving clearance date. Occupational therapy can help adapt daily routines and the home.

after.title: Safety at home and outside
after.text: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

before.title: Understand the sequence
before.text: Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and follow-up have different jobs. Ask your team to draw the intended sequence and identify where you are now. Concurrent treatment means treatments overlap; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment. A change of phase may change the dose, blood tests and support medicines.

after.title: Understand the sequence
after.text: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

before.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
before.text: Ask whether the aim is to control the tumour, delay growth, relieve symptoms, preserve function or a combination of these. Discuss likely benefits, burdens, alternatives and what would prompt a pause or stop. The answer depends on the exact diagnosis, previous treatment and your priorities.

after.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
after.text: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

before.title: Put evidence in context
before.text: Clinical trials describe groups of people and may use older pathology names or different schedules. They cannot predict one person’s response or lifespan. Ask how closely the evidence matches your tumour and treatment. No benefit number from one schedule should automatically be applied to another.

after.title: Put evidence in context
after.text: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

before.title: Discuss options available to you
before.text: Ask about appropriate clinical trials, specialist opinions, symptom support and other treatment options. A medicine or device described in an international guide is not automatically licensed, funded or suitable in Ireland. The treating multidisciplinary team explains what is available and relevant.

after.title: Discuss options available to you
after.text: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

before.title: Make room for your priorities
before.text: Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence, family time, work, travel and side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for information at a pace and in a format that suits you. You may ask for a trusted person to join the discussion, written notes and time to reconsider decisions.

after.title: Make room for your priorities
after.text: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

before.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
before.text: Tell the team about word-finding, attention, memory, reading, vision or planning difficulties. Rehabilitation may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, or neuropsychological support. Written routines, rest breaks and help with medicine organisation can make day-to-day care more manageable.

after.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
after.text: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

before.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
before.text: Report poor appetite, weight change, vomiting or constipation early. Ask for dietitian help if eating is difficult. Use the prescribed anti-sickness and bowel plan; do not wait until symptoms are severe. Choose activity that is safe for your balance and strength and balance it with rest. Ask about treatable causes of fatigue.

after.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
after.text: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

before.title: Emotional support and carers
before.text: Anxiety, low mood, changes in behaviour and uncertainty can affect both patients and carers. Tell the team what has changed and ask for appropriate psychological or social support. Carers may need their own information, practical help and breaks. Agree who the team may share information with.

after.title: Emotional support and carers
after.text: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

before.title: Work, transport and finances
before.text: Ask the specialist nurse or social worker about getting to treatment, time off work, benefits, caring responsibilities and support at home. Plan who can help with daily capsules and appointments if your memory, vision or fatigue makes these difficult.

after.title: Work, transport and finances
after.text: Plan travel, time away from work, caring duties and help with appointments. A nurse or social worker can identify practical support; agree who can help with tablets if needed.

before.title: Supportive care and future wishes
before.text: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life while active treatment continues. You can discuss future care preferences and who you want involved in decisions at a time that suits you. Ask the team for Irish advice and documentation rather than using legal or hospice rules from a US booklet.

after.title: Supportive care and future wishes
after.text: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

before.title: Information that works on paper
before.text: Keep the printed schedule, current medicine list, tests, contact numbers and emergency instructions together. This handbook can be read in sequence without internet access. The wallet card and optional QR code help others find the regimen information; they do not replace your prescription or emergency plan.

after.title: Information that works on paper
after.text: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

before.title: Steroid and seizure plans
before.text: Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

after.title: Steroid and seizure plans
after.text: If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

before.title: Help with the daily plan
before.text: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.

after.title: Help with the daily plan
after.text: Agree who can help with medicines, travel and appointments if memory, sight, fatigue or hand strength makes them difficult. Record your preferences and consent for sharing information.

before.title: When to seek help
before.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

after.title: When to seek help
after.text: Use your written emergency plan even on days without chemotherapy. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow any existing seizure rescue plan. Promptly report worsening headache, repeated vomiting, cough, breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin or eyes, or inability to drink. A held chemotherapy dose must not be restarted without instructions.

before.title: Support medicines
before.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. The team reviews infection and PJP risk, especially with steroids, low lymphocytes or prolonged treatment. A separate prevention prescription may be needed; do not assume the mandatory concurrent-radiotherapy plan automatically applies to this five-day schedule. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

after.title: Support medicines
after.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids. The team reviews infection and PJP risk, especially with steroids, low lymphocytes or prolonged treatment. A separate prevention prescription may be needed; do not assume the mandatory concurrent-radiotherapy plan automatically applies to this five-day schedule. Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting. If prescribed, keep steroids and seizure medicines on separate written schedules. Chemotherapy rest days do not tell you when to stop them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions and explain any dose changes.

before.title: The name and location
before.text: Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different diagnoses. A tumour that spread to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and is not covered by these glioma regimens. Record the exact integrated diagnosis and where it is located.

after.title: The name and location
after.text: A glioma is a tumour arising in the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different types. Cancer that travels to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and follows a different pathway.

before.title: Grade is not the same as stage
before.text: Grade describes features linked to how a tumour behaves. Adult gliomas are usually discussed by their type, grade and molecular findings rather than the stage system used for many other cancers. Grade 4 does not mean cancer has spread through the body. Ask your specialist to explain your own report and any older terminology in the treatment protocol.

after.title: Grade is not the same as stage
after.text: Glioma reports combine the tumour type, grade and molecular findings. Grade is not a measure of spread around the body: a grade 4 brain tumour does not mean body-wide metastases. Ask your specialist to explain older terms in your records.

before.title: IDH and 1p/19q
before.text: IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts of chromosomes 1p and 19q help classify particular gliomas. The combination of findings matters: one result should not be read in isolation. These tests are usually performed on tumour tissue. They do not automatically mean a change has been inherited or that relatives need testing.

after.title: IDH and 1p/19q
after.text: Changes in the IDH genes and loss of chromosome regions 1p and 19q help classify certain gliomas. The pattern of results matters. These are usually tumour-sample tests; they do not by themselves show that a change runs in the family.

before.title: MGMT promoter methylation
before.text: MGMT is involved in repairing certain DNA damage. Methylation of its promoter can reduce that repair activity and helps the team discuss the likely benefit of temozolomide in relevant settings. It is not a blood tumour marker, a percentage of tumour left, or an individual survival prediction. Record the reported result and ask how it affects your treatment choice.

after.title: MGMT promoter methylation
after.text: The MGMT gene makes a protein that repairs a particular type of DNA damage. Methylation in its control region can reduce that repair and inform discussion of temozolomide benefit. This is a tumour-tissue result, not a blood marker or a personal survival percentage.

before.title: A useful diagnosis record
before.text: Keep the biopsy or operation date, pathology wording, grade, IDH result, 1p/19q result and MGMT result if tested. Mark a result as pending or not applicable rather than assuming it is negative. Ask whether specialist pathology review or further testing would change the plan.

after.title: A useful diagnosis record
after.text: Keep the exact pathology diagnosis, sample date, grade and available molecular results together. Label a result as pending or not tested when appropriate. Ask whether further pathology review would affect the plan.

before.title: Safety blood tests
before.text: A full blood count checks infection-fighting white cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets that help stop bleeding. Kidney and liver tests help assess treatment safety. Attend the regimen’s required tests even when you feel well; a reassuring scan does not replace them. The schedule in this guide separates checks before, during and after treatment.

after.title: Safety blood tests
after.text: A full blood count measures red cells, white cells and platelets. Kidney and liver tests assess other aspects of treatment safety. Follow the blood-test schedule even when you feel well or the scan is reassuring.

before.title: MRI and neurological review
before.text: MRI is the main scan used to assess many gliomas. Your team also considers symptoms, strength, movement, speech, memory, daily function and medicines such as steroids. Tell staff before MRI about implants or metal, kidney problems, previous contrast reactions or difficulty lying still. Ask about support if scans make you anxious.

after.title: MRI and neurological review
after.text: MRI gives detailed pictures of the brain. The team also checks symptoms, movement, speech, thinking and daily function. Before scanning, tell staff about implants, metal, kidney problems or previous contrast reactions, and ask for help if the scan worries you.

before.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
before.text: After treatment, inflammation and other treatment effects can resemble tumour growth on MRI. This is sometimes called pseudoprogression. The team may need comparison scans, specialist imaging or further assessment before deciding what a change means. New or worsening symptoms still need prompt review; do not assume they are harmless treatment effects.

after.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
after.text: Treatment-related changes can resemble tumour growth on MRI; this is called pseudoprogression. The specialist interprets the scan with symptoms and may need another scan or further assessment. Report worsening symptoms promptly rather than assuming a scan change is harmless.

before.title: An individual follow-up timetable
before.text: Write the next MRI date, what question it should answer and who will explain the result. Timing depends on your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous findings. General follow-up intervals in an international booklet are not automatically your schedule. These regimens do not require a generic CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or a blood tumour marker before every cycle.

after.title: An individual follow-up timetable
after.text: Record the next MRI and the contact who will explain it. Your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous results determine the interval. Other scans or blood markers are ordered for a specific reason, not automatically before every cycle.

before.title: Keep results with decisions
before.text: Use the passport to distinguish a test being booked, completed and reviewed. Record the agreed next step and whom to call if an appointment or result is missing. Do not alter chemotherapy or steroids yourself in response to a number or scan report.

after.title: Keep results with decisions
after.text: Mark tests as booked, done and reviewed so the next action is clear. Contact the named service about a missing result. Do not change chemotherapy or steroids in response to a report without instructions.

before.title: Know your usual symptoms
before.text: Write down your usual headache, strength, walking, speech, vision, memory, mood, sleep and seizure pattern before treatment. Note new changes, when they started and how they affect daily tasks. With your permission, a trusted person can help spot changes or record what happened.

after.title: Know your usual symptoms
after.text: Before treatment, note your usual walking, strength, speech, sight, memory, sleep and seizure pattern. Record new changes and their timing. A trusted person can help if you want them involved.

before.title: Urgent neurological changes
before.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.

after.title: Urgent neurological changes
after.text: Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice, including on treatment rest days. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. Follow the emergency instructions in any established seizure rescue plan.

before.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
before.text: Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swelling around the tumour. They are not automatically needed for everyone. Ask for the exact dose, time, review date and any taper plan. Do not stop or change them suddenly without advice. Report sleep or mood changes, increased thirst, infection symptoms or muscle weakness and ask which additional checks or protection you need.

after.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
after.text: Steroids may reduce swelling around a brain tumour. If needed, ask for a written dose, review date and reduction plan; do not stop suddenly or adjust the dose yourself. Report infection symptoms, marked thirst, weakness or troublesome sleep or mood changes.

before.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
before.text: If prescribed, take seizure medicines on the agreed schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and whom to contact for breakthrough symptoms. Some medicines can affect mood, alertness or interact with treatment. Do not start, stop or switch them yourself. A rescue medicine needs an individual plan and training for whoever may give it.

after.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
after.text: Take prescribed seizure medicine on its own schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and how to manage a breakthrough seizure. Do not switch or stop it yourself. Anyone giving a rescue medicine needs the personal instructions and training.

before.title: Safety at home and outside
before.text: Ask your clinical team about driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery in light of your symptoms and any seizures. Local medical and licensing rules need individual advice; this guide does not give a universal driving clearance date. Occupational therapy can help adapt daily routines and the home.

after.title: Safety at home and outside
after.text: Discuss driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery with your team, taking account of symptoms and seizures. Individual medical and licensing advice is needed. Occupational therapy can help make daily routines safer.

before.title: Understand the sequence
before.text: Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and follow-up have different jobs. Ask your team to draw the intended sequence and identify where you are now. Concurrent treatment means treatments overlap; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment. A change of phase may change the dose, blood tests and support medicines.

after.title: Understand the sequence
after.text: Place biopsy or surgery, radiotherapy, medicines and follow-up on one plan. Concurrent means treatments overlap; adjuvant means treatment follows the main treatment. A new phase can require different doses, tests and support medicines.

before.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
before.text: Ask whether the aim is to control the tumour, delay growth, relieve symptoms, preserve function or a combination of these. Discuss likely benefits, burdens, alternatives and what would prompt a pause or stop. The answer depends on the exact diagnosis, previous treatment and your priorities.

after.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
after.text: Ask what treatment can reasonably achieve for your tumour and which effects matter most to you. Discuss benefits, burdens, alternatives and the reasons for a pause or stop.

before.title: Put evidence in context
before.text: Clinical trials describe groups of people and may use older pathology names or different schedules. They cannot predict one person’s response or lifespan. Ask how closely the evidence matches your tumour and treatment. No benefit number from one schedule should automatically be applied to another.

after.title: Put evidence in context
after.text: A study result applies to a particular group, diagnosis and schedule. Older studies may use different tumour names. Ask which evidence fits your plan; an average cannot forecast your response or lifespan.

before.title: Discuss options available to you
before.text: Ask about appropriate clinical trials, specialist opinions, symptom support and other treatment options. A medicine or device described in an international guide is not automatically licensed, funded or suitable in Ireland. The treating multidisciplinary team explains what is available and relevant.

after.title: Discuss options available to you
after.text: Ask about suitable trials, another specialist opinion and other treatment or symptom-care options. Your multidisciplinary team explains what is appropriate and available for you.

before.title: Make room for your priorities
before.text: Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence, family time, work, travel and side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for information at a pace and in a format that suits you. You may ask for a trusted person to join the discussion, written notes and time to reconsider decisions.

after.title: Make room for your priorities
after.text: Bring up thinking, independence, family time, work and the side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for time, written notes or a supporter if that helps you weigh the choices.

before.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
before.text: Tell the team about word-finding, attention, memory, reading, vision or planning difficulties. Rehabilitation may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, or neuropsychological support. Written routines, rest breaks and help with medicine organisation can make day-to-day care more manageable.

after.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
after.text: Tell the team about changes in memory, language, attention, sight or planning. Rehabilitation can involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy or psychology. Ask for practical help with routines and medicines.

before.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
before.text: Report poor appetite, weight change, vomiting or constipation early. Ask for dietitian help if eating is difficult. Use the prescribed anti-sickness and bowel plan; do not wait until symptoms are severe. Choose activity that is safe for your balance and strength and balance it with rest. Ask about treatable causes of fatigue.

after.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
after.text: Use your prescribed nausea and bowel plan and report problems early. Ask for dietitian help if intake or weight falls. Adapt movement to your balance and strength, and ask the team to assess fatigue that disrupts daily life.

before.title: Emotional support and carers
before.text: Anxiety, low mood, changes in behaviour and uncertainty can affect both patients and carers. Tell the team what has changed and ask for appropriate psychological or social support. Carers may need their own information, practical help and breaks. Agree who the team may share information with.

after.title: Emotional support and carers
after.text: Tell the team about changes in mood, behaviour or coping. Patients and carers may each need psychological or practical support. Agree who can receive information and ask for help before caring becomes overwhelming.

before.title: Work, transport and finances
before.text: Ask the specialist nurse or social worker about getting to treatment, time off work, benefits, caring responsibilities and support at home. Plan who can help with daily capsules and appointments if your memory, vision or fatigue makes these difficult.

after.title: Work, transport and finances
after.text: Plan travel, time away from work, caring duties and help with appointments. A nurse or social worker can identify practical support; agree who can help with tablets if needed.

before.title: Supportive care and future wishes
before.text: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life while active treatment continues. You can discuss future care preferences and who you want involved in decisions at a time that suits you. Ask the team for Irish advice and documentation rather than using legal or hospice rules from a US booklet.

after.title: Supportive care and future wishes
after.text: Supportive and palliative care can help manage symptoms while treatment continues. When you are ready, discuss future care preferences and whom you want involved. Ask your team to help document these wishes.

before.title: Information that works on paper
before.text: Keep the printed schedule, current medicine list, tests, contact numbers and emergency instructions together. This handbook can be read in sequence without internet access. The wallet card and optional QR code help others find the regimen information; they do not replace your prescription or emergency plan.

after.title: Information that works on paper
after.text: Keep the latest paper schedule, medicine list, results plan and emergency contacts together. The treatment card helps others identify your regimen. It supports, but does not replace, the prescription and emergency instructions.

before.title: Appointments and supply
before.text: Arrange blood tests, transport, medicine supply and interpreter or carer support. Check who reviews results and how you receive the decision before the next dose.

after.title: Appointments and supply
after.text: Before each visit, check four things: the blood-test booking, how you will get there, your medicine supply and any help you need. Ask who will review the results and tell you whether the next dose can go ahead.

before.title: Paper copies and contacts
before.text: Keep the full handbook, three-page summary and wallet card together. The QR code is optional. Ask the team to replace every labelled example contact with your real oncology and out-of-hours details; ask for a new printed plan when treatment changes.

after.title: Paper copies and contacts
after.text: Keep the handbook, short guide and treatment card in one place. Ask your team to fill in the real daytime and emergency numbers and print a replacement when the plan changes. A phone is optional.

before.title: Your diagnosis and stage
before.text: Keep the pathology report, original melanoma site, stage and known sites of spread. This guide concerns advanced disease that cannot be removed completely by surgery or has spread; it does not describe a postoperative recurrence-prevention course.

after.title: Your diagnosis and stage
after.text: Record where the melanoma began, its pathology result and the sites involved now. This pathway treats melanoma that cannot be fully removed or has spread. Treatment after complete removal has a different aim and a separate plan.

before.title: The tumour test
before.text: A BRAF V600 test helps identify whether BRAF-targeted medicines are an option. A tumour mutation does not by itself mean an inherited family condition. Keep the exact result and ask how it changes your choices.

after.title: The tumour test
after.text: The laboratory checks a sample of the melanoma for a BRAF V600 change. The result can identify a target for certain medicines. A change found in the tumour does not, by itself, establish an inherited condition.

before.title: Scans and local treatments
before.text: Record the scans used to follow known disease. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role for a particular site; ask for their timing and risks to be added to the overall plan.

after.title: Scans and local treatments
after.text: Add planned scans, any operation and any radiotherapy to the same calendar. Ask what each part is intended to achieve and which team arranges it.

before.title: New changes still matter
before.text: Report a new lump, changing mole, persistent skin sore or unexplained symptom. A response at one site does not establish that every other symptom is harmless.

after.title: New changes still matter
after.text: Tell your team about a changing mole, a persistent sore, a new lump or an unexplained symptom. Improvement in a known tumour does not explain a new problem elsewhere.

before.title: Practical arrangements
before.text: Know where and when bloods are taken, how results reach the prescriber, and how to obtain the next supply or appointment. Ask for written instructions in a format you can use without a phone.

after.title: Practical arrangements
after.text: Write down where blood samples are taken, who receives the results and how you obtain the next appointment or medicine supply. Request a printed plan if that is easier to use.

before.title: When life is affected
before.text: Tell the team about fatigue, pain, appetite, sleep, mood and ability to work or care for others. Practical and supportive care can accompany anticancer treatment; you do not have to wait until treatment ends.

after.title: When life is affected
after.text: Bring up difficulties with eating, sleep, pain, energy, work or caring for someone. The team can arrange symptom support while cancer treatment continues.

before.title: Food, fluids and activity
before.text: Keep meals and fluids manageable and follow any individual fluid or diet restrictions. Gentle activity and rest can be adjusted to how you feel. Ask for dietetic or rehabilitation help if intake, weight, strength or mobility is falling.

after.title: Food, fluids and activity
after.text: Choose food, fluids and movement that you can manage, within any personal restrictions. Ask for help early if you are losing weight, drinking less or finding everyday activity harder.

before.title: Sexual health
before.text: Tell the team about sexual symptoms, relationship concerns or practical difficulties with the agreed precautions. Ask for a private discussion and specialist support when needed.

after.title: Sexual health
after.text: You can request a private discussion about intimacy, sexual symptoms or relationships. Ask for help if the agreed pregnancy precautions are difficult to follow.

before.title: Support alongside treatment
before.text: Ask about symptom control, psychological support, finances, transport, work and help at home. Palliative or supportive care can be used alongside anticancer treatment to improve comfort and function.

after.title: Support alongside treatment
after.text: Supportive care addresses symptoms and daily life during cancer treatment. Palliative care can be part of that support; accepting it does not mean you must stop anticancer treatment.

before.title: A person you trust
before.text: If helpful, bring a family member or supporter and agree what information may be shared. Ask for an interpreter or accessible information when needed; use teach-back to check the schedule and urgent plan.

after.title: A person you trust
after.text: Choose whether to involve a relative or supporter and what may be shared with them. Ask for an interpreter or a different information format. Check that you can explain the next dose, tests and urgent-contact plan in your own words.

before.title: Your document set
before.text: Keep consent information, the three-page summary, complete handbook, treatment card, test plan and real contact details together. The QR opens more information but essential instructions remain available in print.

after.title: Your document set
after.text: Keep the current treatment summary, medicine list, test plan and contact card together. Use the printed instructions when you need them; the QR code is an optional link to further information.

before.title: A treatment summary
before.text: Record medicines and doses received, important side effects, admissions, last-dose date, ongoing symptom treatment and the clinician responsible for follow-up. Ask for an updated paper copy for your GP and other treating teams.

after.title: A treatment summary
after.text: Ask for a treatment summary showing what you received, important side effects, admissions, the last dose and the follow-up team. Share the current version with your GP and other clinicians.

before.title: Your next review
before.text: Confirm the next blood test, scan and review, who explains the result, and which symptoms should trigger contact sooner. Keep actual daytime and out-of-hours numbers accessible after treatment stops.

after.title: Your next review
after.text: Before leaving, confirm the next test and review, how you will receive results and whom to call sooner. Keep those numbers available after treatment ends.

before.title: Support for neurological symptoms
before.text: Keep any prescribed seizure medicine and steroid plan separate from the PCV calendar. Report new weakness, tingling, gait change or constipation before vincristine. A medicine review is needed before adding any treatment for symptoms.

after.title: Support for neurological symptoms
after.text: Keep prescribed steroids and seizure medicines on a separate plan from chemotherapy. Before vincristine, report new weakness, tingling, walking difficulty or constipation. Check new symptom medicines with the team.
